name: The Doubled Eye

stars.name: Geminus Alpha
stars.notes: Identical to its twin in every measurable property—mass, luminosity, chemical composition, rotation period, starspot patterns. Statistically impossible.

stars.name: Geminus Beta
stars.notes: Mirrors Geminus Alpha exactly. Even transient phenomena—flares, coronal mass ejections—occur simultaneously in both stars.

planets.name: Echo-A
planets.notes: Orbits Geminus Alpha at 0.3 AU. Geological surveys show it is compositionally identical to Echo-B orbiting the other star.

planets.name: Echo-B
planets.notes: Orbits Geminus Beta at 0.3 AU. A mirror of Echo-A down to crater distribution patterns. Researchers cannot determine which is the 'original.'

planets.name: Reflection
planets.notes: Circumbinary orbit at 4.1 AU. Atmosphere is breathable but lifeless. Surface features display bilateral symmetry along a north-south axis.

planets.name: Singular
planets.notes: The only body in the system that does not exhibit mirroring. Researchers consider it the most important object here precisely because it breaks the pattern.

anomalies.name: The Synchrony
anomalies.location: Between Geminus Alpha and Geminus Beta
anomalies.notes: Both stars exhibit simultaneous identical behavior despite 48 AU separation. Flares, luminosity fluctuations, and even individual starspot emergence are perfectly synchronized with zero measurable delay.

anomalies.name: The Mirror Effect
anomalies.notes: Echo-A and Echo-B are identical to molecular resolution. Isotope ratios, crystal structures, even the distribution of surface boulders above 1 meter match. No natural process can account for this precision.

anomalies.name: Singular's Exemption
anomalies.notes: The outermost planet alone is asymmetric and unique. Some researchers theorize it predates whatever process created the symmetry, while others believe it was deliberately left as a control variable.

asteroid_belts.name: The Divided Belt
asteroid_belts.location: Between the inner pairs and Reflection, 1.5-2.8 AU
asteroid_belts.notes: The belt is split into two identical halves. Asteroids on each side mirror the mass, composition, and trajectory of a counterpart on the other. Collisions between mirrored pairs have never been observed.

stations.name: Parallax Observatory
stations.notes: University of Valen research outpost. Crew rotates every six months. Several researchers have reported psychological distress related to prolonged exposure to the system's symmetry.

faction_control.notes: Designated an open research zone by interstellar treaty. The University of Valen holds the only active research permit.

history: Discovered in 2501 by the deep-space survey vessel Calloway. Initial reports of a 'perfectly matched binary' were treated as calibration error until follow-up missions confirmed the symmetry.

The 2514 Geminus Expedition spent eighteen months mapping both stars and inner planets, producing the landmark paper 'Mirror Stars: Implications for Stellar Formation Theory.' No formation theory has successfully explained the findings.
In 2529, researcher Dr. Orin Sahl reported that the planet Singular appeared to be 2.1 billion years older than the rest of the system. His data has been disputed but never disproven.
description: The Doubled Eye is a binary system that defies probability. Its two stars, Geminus Alpha and Geminus Beta, are not merely similar—they are identical in every property that can be measured, from mass and luminosity to the precise timing of stellar flares. They orbit a common center at 48 AU separation, each hosting a small rocky planet that mirrors the other in composition, geology, and even surface boulder distribution. A third world orbits both stars and displays its own unsettling bilateral symmetry.

The central mystery is the mechanism of synchronization. The two stars behave as if they are a single object observed from two positions, yet they are demonstrably separate bodies separated by billions of kilometers. Information cannot travel between them fast enough to explain the simultaneous flare events. The mirrored planets compound the impossibility—identical worlds around identical stars, as if the system were folded along an invisible axis. Whatever process created this arrangement operates outside known physics.

Singular, the outermost planet, is the key that most researchers want to turn. It alone breaks the system's perfect symmetry, and if Dr. Sahl's age estimates are correct, it existed before the mirroring began. A mission to core-sample Singular's deep geology could reveal whether the duplication was a single event or an ongoing process. The Parallax Observatory crew reports that their instruments occasionally detect faint gravitational pulses originating from the exact geometric center of the two stars—a point in empty space where nothing should exist.
